title: Read a Roman Numeral
statement:
Roman numerals use seven letters: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000.

Letters are usually written from largest to smallest and simply added up. The exception: a smaller letter placed directly before a larger one is subtracted instead. Only six such pairs exist: IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), XC (90), CD (400) and CM (900).

Given a valid numeral s for a number from 1 to 3999, return its value.

examples.why: Every letter is no smaller than the one after it, so just add: 50 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
X comes before the larger L, so it counts as −10: −10 + 50 + 1 + 1. Adding every letter would give 62.

constraints: s is a valid numeral for a value in [1, 3999]
hints: Without the subtraction pairs, the answer is just the sum of the letter values. What tells you a letter is part of a subtraction pair?
A letter is subtracted exactly when the next letter is worth more.
Walk left to right. If the value of s[i] is less than the value of s[i + 1], subtract it; otherwise add it.

explain.intuition:
In a normal numeral the values never increase from left to right. A subtraction pair is the only place where a small letter sits right before a bigger one. So you do not need a list of the six special pairs at all: compare each letter with its right neighbour.

If the neighbour is bigger, this letter is the "minus" half of a pair, so subtract it. Otherwise add it. The bigger letter in the pair is then added normally on its own turn, and the pair works out: XL becomes −10 + 50 = 40.
steps: Map each letter to its value.
For each index i, let v be the value of s[i].
If i + 1 < n and the next value is bigger than v, subtract v; otherwise add it.
pitfalls: Comparing with the previous letter but forgetting to undo the amount already added for it (you would need to subtract it twice).
Reading past the end of the string when checking the next letter.

solutions.title: Match the six pairs first
solutions.idea: At each position, check whether the next two letters form one of the six subtraction pairs. If so, add the pair's value and jump two; otherwise add the single letter.

solutions.title: Compare with the next letter
solutions.idea: A letter is subtracted exactly when the letter after it is worth more. No pair table needed.

followups: The input may be invalid, like "IIII" or "IC". How would you reject it?
Go the other way: turn a number into a numeral.
